newsitem.title: FRANCE: French jobless stable despite May jump-economists.
newsitem.headline: French jobless stable despite May jump-economists.

text.p: French unemployment is stabilising despite a big jump in May's jobless total, economists said on Monday.
But they forecast unemployment would likely not start falling until toward year-end or early 1998 and could even nudge up a little in the months ahead.

Seasonally adjusted figures released on Monday by the employment ministry showed the number of people out of work climbed by 32,400 or 1.1 percent to 3,113,500. It was the biggest monthly rise since October 1993 and reversed three successive months of falls.
The unemployment rate calculated according to International Labour Organisation methods, which differ from those of the ministry, was unchanged at 12.5 percent.
"I don't think one should make too much of the May rise," said David Naude of JP Morgan. "The average over the last few months says the trend in unemployment is stabilising."
"There is a cyclical pickup in the economy. We're bound to see a very strong second quarter," he added.

This more robust growth, he said, would translate into lower unemployment "but only slowly and progressively. I do not expect unemployment to decline until well into the second half or perhaps early next year."
Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said despite the large May jump, "when you look at the trend, the rate of deterioration in unemployment has slowed".

"We expect stabilisation of unemployment at current levels and it to start falling next year," she said, adding the general rule was that the economy needed to generate annual growth of at least two-and-half percent to see a drop in unemployment.
The previous conservative government, ousted in the June 1 parliamentary election, said it expected growth would be at least 2.3 percent in 1997 and a minimum 2.8 percent next year.
"The important thing is there has been a declining trend over the last six months," Eric Muller of UBS.
Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley called the rise a "blip".
"Leading short term indicators are positive, the number of business start-ups are rising, and the number of temporary jobs is rising which is a very accurate indicator of what is happening," he said.
Unemployment would edge down to 12.3 percent by year end and to fall below 12 percent next year, helped by stronger growth, he forecast.
He said nonetheless the May rise was large and would "put pressure on the government to take action on unemployment".
The Socialists swept to power on a pledge to make fighting unemployment its top priority and ruled out further austerity for France to qualify for Europe's planned new single currency.
But reports suggesting France's public deficit in 1997 could sharply overshoot conditions for qualifying for monetary union had limited the government's scope for action, economists said.
"Employment policies will at best be neutral given budget restraints. They will do things to reallocate spending rather than increase spending." said JP Morgan's Naude.
The task of cutting unemployment had been made even tougher by a growing labour force, economists said.
